title: The Translator Who Invented Zero's Journey West
event_summary: In the late 12th century, the young Italian merchant Leonardo of Pisa (later called Fibonacci) studied under Muslim mathematicians in the thriving port city of Béjaïa in what is now Algeria. His unnamed Algerian tutor—likely a scholar in the city's robust tradition of Hindu-Arabic mathematical practice—taught him the decimal positional number system including the concept of zero, methods of calculation that had been refined by generations of Maghrebi scholars building on al-Khwarizmi's work. Without this specific intellectual encounter in Béjaïa, Fibonacci's 1202 book Liber Abaci would never have been written, and Europe's adoption of the number system that now underpins all modern computation would have been delayed by generations.
why_forgotten: European accounts credited Fibonacci as a lone genius while erasing his North African teachers entirely. Colonial-era historiography systematically minimized the intellectual achievements of the Maghreb, and Béjaïa's once-famous scholarly tradition was obscured after centuries of political upheaval. The unnamed tutor became a footnote—if mentioned at all—in a story reframed as European self-discovery.
why_it_matters: Every digital transaction, every line of computer code, every scientific equation written today uses the numeral system that entered Europe through this specific North African transmission point. Béjaïa's scholars were the critical human link in a chain of knowledge stretching from India through Baghdad to the modern world, yet the city receives virtually no recognition for enabling the mathematical foundation of global civilization.
